M6-01-MULTIPLIDITRANSAZIONE.5:
## A transaction multiple isn't a trading multiple

A trading multiple comes from the price of a single share, traded on the stock market by investors buying a liquid minority stake. A **transaction** multiple comes from what a buyer paid for 100% of a company, i.e. for **control**: appointing management, deciding strategy, disposing of cash. Control has a price, and the premium shows in the multiple.

Watch the numerator. The price you read in the press release is the one paid to shareholders for the equity; but the buyer also takes on the target's net debt. The transaction's EV/EBITDA multiple is calculated on EV, not on the equity price.

**The deal.** Target in the {sector} sector, EBITDA {p1}, net debt {p2}. Price paid for 100% of the equity: {p3}. In the same period the sector was trading on the stock market at {p4} EV/EBITDA.

M6-02-PREMIOCONTROLLO.2: In {B_PREMIO} the implied premium on the multiple in the comparable deal: by what percentage the multiple paid ({B_MULT_TRANSAZIONE_OSS}) exceeds the target's trading multiple before the announcement ({B_MULT_TRADING_PRE}).
M6-02-PREMIOCONTROLLO.3: In {B_MULT_IMPLICITO} the reverse exercise: the plausible transaction multiple for the new target, applying the premium just extracted to its current trading multiple ({B_MULT_TRADING_NUOVO}). Reuse cell {B_PREMIO}, don't retype the number.
M6-02-PREMIOCONTROLLO.4:
## The control premium: extracting and applying it

The previous level showed the raw fact: a transaction multiple always exceeds the trading multiple of the same target, in the same period. Here that fact becomes a USABLE NUMBER, the implied premium on the multiple as a percentage — and it's used in TWO opposite DIRECTIONS. Mind the name: the **control premium** strictly speaking is measured on the price per share (equity); what you read on the EV/EBITDA multiple is its reflection on the whole company, and the two numbers coincide only if the company has no debt.

**Extracting (T1).** From a deal that has already happened, how much the buyer paid ABOVE the price at which the target was trading on the market BEFORE the deal was announced. The benchmark is PRE-announcement trading: after the announcement the share price already jumps to price in the expected deal, so comparing with that would understate the premium really paid.

**Applying (T2, reverse exercise).** Taking that percentage premium as a market reference, you estimate a plausible transaction multiple for a NEW target, never involved in any deal — multiplying its current trading multiple by (1 + premium). It's exactly the reasoning of a pitch: "comparable deals paid a 20-25% premium over pre-announcement trading; our target trades today at a certain multiple; a plausible buyer might pay around that multiple increased by the same premium".

**The comparable deal.** A target in the {sector1} sector was trading on the market at {p1} EV/EBITDA before the deal was announced. The buyer then paid for 100% of the target at a transaction multiple of {p2}.

**The new target.** A hypothetical target in the {sector2} sector, never involved in any M&A transaction, trades today on the market at {p4} EV/EBITDA.

M6-03-SINERGIENELPREZZO.2: In {B_PREMIO_SINERGIE} break out the premium for expected synergies, in %: it's the part of the TOTAL control premium actually paid in the deal ({B_PREMIO_TOTALE}) that EXCEEDS the pure-control benchmark ({B_PREMIO_PURO}) — what is typically paid ONLY for the right to be in charge, in comparable deals with no particular synergies expected. Subtract the benchmark from the total paid: {B_PREMIO_TOTALE}-{B_PREMIO_PURO}. The result is always positive: it's the share of the premium the buyer "gave away" to the seller, betting on achieving enough synergies to pay it back — synergies that, at signing, are still a promise, not a fact.
M6-03-SINERGIENELPREZZO.3: In {B_SINERGIE_EUR} turn the synergy premium into a number that hurts: multiply the synergy premium just calculated ({B_PREMIO_SINERGIE}) by the target's equity value BEFORE the deal ({B_EQUITY_PRE}). Formula: {B_PREMIO_SINERGIE}*{B_EQUITY_PRE}. That amount in euros is exactly what the buyer bet it would achieve in real synergies after closing — cost integration, cross-selling, greater pricing power. If it doesn't, that amount is the part of the price paid for a company that, for them, wasn't worth that much: they paid more than the target was worth without the promised synergies.
M6-03-SINERGIENELPREZZO.4:
## Synergies already given away in the price

The previous level isolated the control premium as ONE number. Here that number splits into two pieces that are NOT the same thing.

**Pure control.** What a buyer typically pays ONLY for the right to be in charge — appointing management, deciding strategy, disposing of cash — WITHOUT expecting particular synergies from that specific combination. It's a benchmark observable across a set of "generic" comparable deals.

**Expected synergies.** The part of the TOTAL premium paid in a specific deal that EXCEEDS that benchmark. It's the share the buyer "gave away" to the seller, betting on achieving enough synergies to pay it back — synergies that, at signing, are still a PROMISE, not a fact. If they don't materialise, that part of the price was paid for a company that, for the buyer, wasn't worth that much.

**The deal.** The target had an equity value of {p0} before the deal was announced. The buyer paid a TOTAL control premium of {p1}. The pure-control benchmark for comparable deals with no particular synergies expected, in the same period, is {p2}.

M6-04-ANNOUNCEDCOMPLETED.2: In {B_MULT_ANNUNCIO} the EV/EBITDA multiple implied by the price per share offered at announcement. EV is the equity offered for all the shares plus the net debt the buyer takes on.
M6-04-ANNOUNCEDCOMPLETED.3: In {B_MULT_COMPLETAMENTO} the same multiple with the price per share actually paid at closing: shares, net debt and EBITDA don't change, only the price does.
M6-04-ANNOUNCEDCOMPLETED.4: In {B_VARIAZIONE} the percentage change in the multiple from announcement to completion. It can come out positive or negative: an M&A database reporting only a deal's "announced" multiple can have you read a number the market never actually paid. Typical reasons why the two numbers differ: a price renegotiation after announcement (often due to due diligence findings), payment wholly or partly in the buyer's shares whose value moves between announcement and closing, or conditions precedent (antitrust clearance, shareholder approvals) that change the final terms versus those announced.
M6-04-ANNOUNCEDCOMPLETED.5:
## Announced vs completed: the multiple moves over time

A transaction multiple read from an M&A database is almost always calculated on a price — but A deal has two relevant prices, not one. The **announced** price is the one declared to the market on the day the transaction is made public. The **completed** (closing) price is the one actually paid on the day the transaction closes — weeks or months later. Between the two moments the terms can change: through a renegotiation (often following due diligence), because payment is wholly or partly in the buyer's shares and their market value has moved in the meantime, or through conditions precedent (antitrust clearance, shareholder approvals) that change the final terms.

The multiple calculated on the announcement price and the one calculated on the closing price are therefore two DIFFERENT numbers for the same transaction, and anyone comparing past deals must know which of the two they're looking at — and how far apart the two are.

**The deal.** The target has {p0} shares outstanding and EBITDA of {p1}, unchanged between announcement and closing, and net debt of {p2} that passes to the buyer. The buyer offered {p3} per share when the deal was announced. At completion, the price actually paid per share was {p4}.

M6-05-CICLODIMERCATO.2: In {B_RAPPORTO} compute the market-cycle adjustment ratio: the sector's market index TODAY ({B_INDICE_OGGI}) divided by the same sector's index IN THE PERIOD of the past deal ({B_INDICE_ALLORA}). A ratio above 1.00x says sector multiples have risen since then (the market has "heated up"); below 1.00x says they've fallen (the market has compressed). It's the factor needed to bring a multiple observed in that period to current market conditions.
M6-05-CICLODIMERCATO.3: In {B_MULTIPLO_AGGIUSTATO} compute the past deal's multiple ADJUSTED for the market cycle: the multiple observed in the deal ({B_MULTIPLO_OSSERVATO}) times the adjustment ratio calculated in the previous task ({B_RAPPORTO}). Careful: this adjustment does NOT change the facts of the deal — the price the buyer actually paid then stays what it was, full stop. What changes is how that multiple should be READ today: the adjusted multiple doesn't represent "how much was paid", but "what an equivalent multiple would be worth under today's market conditions" — the number to compare with comps and other precedents, not the raw historical multiple.
M6-05-CICLODIMERCATO.4:
## Market cycle: a transaction multiple ages with the market

A multiple observed in a past deal isn't just "old" in the calendar sense (that's the announced vs completed problem). It's also old in the sense of the MARKET CYCLE in which it was paid. If that deal closed in a "hot" market (lots of liquidity, lots of competition among buyers, generally high multiples) or, on the contrary, in a crisis (risk aversion, compressed multiples), the observed multiple carries that market condition with it. Comparing it directly with a multiple from today, without adjusting it, risks comparing apples with oranges: the difference you see might reflect only the cycle, not the target's characteristics.

The standard correction: take an indicator of the average level of multiples in the same sector during the past deal's period, and the same indicator measured today. Their ratio says how much the market has moved in the meantime. Multiplying the observed multiple by this ratio gives a "cycle-adjusted" multiple, comparable to today's market conditions.

**The deal.** A past deal in this sector closed at a multiple of {p0}. In the period when that deal closed, the sector's market index (average EV/EBITDA multiple of comparable transactions at the time) was {p1}. The same index, measured today, is {p2}.

M6-06-TRIANGOLAZIONE.2: In {B_AMPIEZZA} compute the WIDTH of the triangulation range: the HIGHEST of the three implied EVs ({rangeValori}) minus the LOWEST — i.e. MAX({rangeValori})-MIN({rangeValori}). It's how wide, in euros, the interval is within which comps, precedents and DCF place the target's Enterprise Value: the wider it is, the less the three methods agree with each other, and the more you need to understand why before using just one.
M6-06-TRIANGOLAZIONE.3: In {B_MEDIA} compute the simple AVERAGE value of the three methods: AVERAGE({rangeValori}). It's a naive summary — it weighs comps, precedents and DCF exactly the same, without knowing whether one of the three is distorted (an unusually hot comps market, a DCF with overly optimistic assumptions, a precedent paid in a market cycle very different from today). It's a starting point for triangulation, not necessarily the number to write in the term sheet.
M6-06-TRIANGOLAZIONE.4: In {B_SCOSTAMENTO_DCF} compute the % DEVIATION of the DCF from the average of comps and precedents — WITHOUT including the DCF in that average (otherwise the DCF would partly be compared with itself): ({B_EV_DCF}-AVERAGE({B_EV_COMPS},{B_EV_PRECEDENTI}))/AVERAGE({B_EV_COMPS},{B_EV_PRECEDENTI}). A positive result says the DCF is worth MORE than the two market-based methods suggest; negative, that it's worth LESS. In either case it's not automatically an error: the DCF reflects internal assumptions (growth, margins, WACC) which by construction needn't match market sentiment — the deviation is the trigger to ask why, not a signal to fix at the desk.
M6-06-TRIANGOLAZIONE.5:
## Triangulation: comps, precedents and DCF that diverge

Three different methods to estimate the same Enterprise Value RARELY produce the same number — and that's not an error to correct, it's information.

**Trading comps** reflect CURRENT market sentiment: an optimistic stock market pushes multiples up even when the target's fundamentals haven't changed one bit; a pessimistic market compresses them just the same.

**Precedents** (the levels of this module) reflect control premiums paid in HISTORICAL transactions — something that really happened, but something from the past, perhaps in a market cycle very different from today's.

**The DCF** (subject of the next module, given here as an input) reflects INTERNAL assumptions — growth, margins, WACC — chosen by whoever builds the model: they can be more or less prudent, and don't depend on the market's mood on a given day.

None of the three is "the right one" by definition. Triangulating doesn't mean picking a winner: it means understanding WHY the three numbers diverge, and which interval actually remains defensible.

**The case.** For the same target, the three methods imply: EV from comps {p0}, EV from precedents {p1}, EV from DCF {p2} (the actual DCF is the subject of the next module: here it arrives already calculated, as data).
